topic: The Bridge Between Slopes and Areas: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

sections.title: Intuitive Hook: The Accumulation Concept
sections.content: Use an animation of a 'Robot Vacuum' moving. Its speed (derivative) creates a path, and the area under the speed-time graph represents the total distance (integral) traveled. This visual establishes the link between 'rate of change' and 'accumulation'.
sections.example: A robot moves at 2m/s for 3 seconds. The area of the rectangle (2x3) equals the total distance (6m).

sections.title: Prerequisite Review: Area as a Function
sections.content: Introduce the area function A(x) = ∫[a to x] f(t) dt. Visualize this as a 'sliding curtain' moving across a graph, covering more area as x increases. This prepares the student to see integration as a dynamic process.
sections.example: Visualize the region under f(t) = 2t being filled with liquid as the right boundary 'x' moves to the right.

sections.title: The Core Connection: Differentiation and Integration
sections.content: Present the derivative of the area function: d/dx [∫[a to x] f(t) dt] = f(x). Graphically show that adding a tiny slice of width Δx adds an area approximately equal to the height f(x) times the width. The rate at which area grows is exactly the height of the curve.
sections.example: If the area under a curve is 'A', then 'dA/dx' is the instantaneous height of the curve at x.

sections.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC)
sections.content: Formalize the theorem: ∫[a to b] f(x)dx = F(b) - F(a), where F' = f. Explain this as the 'inverse' relationship: differentiation strips away the area accumulation, while integration reconstructs the original function from its slope.
sections.example: Calculating the total distance (integral) by looking at the difference in position (antiderivative) at two specific time points.

sections.title: Synthesis and Summary
sections.content: Summarize the cycle: Derivative takes us from position to velocity (steepness), Integral takes us from velocity to position (accumulation). They are two sides of the same mathematical coin.
sections.example: Final animation: A clock hand spinning. Its velocity (derivative) defines its path, and the integral of its velocity over time returns the total angle swept (position).
